data.abstractNote: Down through the years, several scholars have noted the rather curious phenomenon of paired items in Hebrew and Greek appearing in the opposite order in Syriac translations of the Old Testament and New Testament. The present study takes up a particular instance of pair reversal which appears in the Peshitta of Job and 2 Samuel and suggests that it reflects the influence of Greek idiom and perhaps even the New Testament itself on the Syriac translation tradition.

data.title: Tatian and the Jewish Scriptures: A Textual and Philological Analysis of the Old Testament Citations in Tatian’s Diatessaron
data.abstractNote: It has long been recognized that Old Testament citations appear in the Old Syriac Gospels in ways quite different from the way they appear in the Greek Gospels. Because the Old Syriac Gospels stand as witnesses to Tatian's Diatessaron, a second-century Syriac Gospel harmony, it has been argued that this phenomenon of variant Old Testament citations is a characteristic of the Diatessaron, and that the Old Syriac Gospels received these variant citations from the Diatessaron. Moreover, many of the Old Testament citations in the Old Syriac/Diatessaron stand closer to Hebrew text traditions and other Jewish exegetical traditions, a dynamic which has been explained on the theory that Tatian used the Old Testament Peshitta, the Old Testament of the Syriac church (which was translated from the Hebrew Bible), in the creation of the Diatessaron. In this dissertation, I demonstrate on the contrary that when Old Testament citations in the Diatessaron are accurately reconstructed, there is little evidence that Tatian assimilated these citations to the text of the Old Testament Peshitta. Rather, Tatian took over the Old Testament citations in the form he found them in the Gospel sources he used in the creation of the Diatessaron in the second century. Where they vary from the form these citations take in the Greek Gospel tradition, it is because Tatian possessed an earlier form of the Gospel texts than what is preserved in the Greek manuscript tradition of the fourth century and later. In preserving an older, and possibly more original, form of many of these citations, Tatian's Diatessaron stands as an important early witness to the state of the Gospel tradition in the second century and sheds light on the issue of the status and function of the various versions of the Bible in early Syriac Christianity.

data.title: Maternal and Paternal Lineages of Assyrian Population
data.abstractNote: Near East is home to religious minorities whose identities and traditions link them to pre-Islamic, and sometime, pre-Christianity populations. The cultural isolation of these communities is often accompanied by a tradition of endogamy and therefore, these populations are believed to have experienced less admixture compared with other Near Eastern populations. Therefore, studying these minority groups may provide unique insights into the population genetics of the region. This study contributes to our understanding of the population genetics of Near East by exploring mitochondrial and Y-chromosome variation in Assyrian immigrants in the United States. Assyrians are Neo-Aramaic speaking Christians of the Upper Mesopotamia who, prior to the Ottoman Genocide, lived in a territory today divided between northern Iraq, southern Turkey, and northwestern Iran. Much of the curiosity about the origin of Assyrians is due to the antiquity of their language, their religion, and the proximity of their territory to the heartland of ancient Assyria. Focusing on the Assyrian population, this project investigates the role of religion and sociocultural pressures on the genetic substructuring of Near Eastern populations. Taking a genetic approach, this project also contributes to the debate on the origins and early migrations of the Semitic speaking populations. Finally, the genetic data also is used to examine the hypotheses on the origins of Assyrians maternal and paternal lineages.

data.title: Muḍṭariban maǧnūnan: A Case of Phraseology and Evolving Motifs of Literary and Medical Love-Sickness in the Tale of Salāmān and Absāl
data.abstractNote: The Tale of Salāmān and Absāl presented as a translation from Greek, attributed in the text’s opening lines to Ḥunayn b. Isḥāq, is saturated with references from a wide-ranging variety of sources with an array of religious, cultural and textual orientations; these, as well as its generic affiliations, ideological leanings, location on the spiritual-metaphysical spectrum and Vorlagen have been studied by many. In this paper, I focus on the wording and literary forms of the text, some of which have been glossed over in the rendition of Henry Corbin, by which this text is often known. My point of departure is a collocation which draws on motifs and phraseology from popular sources, the canons of poetry and poetry in prose (including belles lettres elements in the Qurʾān), as well as terminology in medical literature in Arabic and Greek traditions. Through an analysis of phrasing drawing on philological methods of Blachère, Von Grunebaum, Arazi and others, a contextualization of this Tale (which is not covered in research on “profane love theory” e.g. by Lois Giffen) may lead to a reading of this Hermetic text within a repertoire of “romantic” commonplaces and innovations of expression.
